Translate it "appointed time" (<reference osisRef="Job.14.14">Job 14:14</reference>). Job reverts to the sad picture of man, however great, which he had drawn (<reference osisRef="Job.3.14">Job 3:14</reference>), and details in this chapter the miseries which his friends will see, if, according to his request (<reference osisRef="Job.6.28">Job 6:28</reference>), they will look on him. entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 7 Job 7:1-21 . Job Excuses His Desire for Death. 1. appointed time-- better, "a warfare," hard conflict with evil (so in Is 40:2 ; Da 10:1 ). Translate it "appointed time" ( Job 14:14 ). Job reverts to the sad picture of man, however great, which he had drawn ( Job 3:14 ), and details in this chapter the miseries which his friends will see, if, according to his request ( Job 6:28 ), they will look on him. Even the Christian soldier, "warring a good warfare," rejoices when it is completed ( 1Ti 1:18 ; 2Ti 2:3 ; 4:7 , 8 ).

entries.content_plain: 2. earnestly desireth-- Hebrew, "pants for the [evening] shadow." Easterners measure time by the length of their shadow. If the servant longs for the evening when his wages are paid, why may not Job long for the close of his hard service, when he shall enter on his "reward?" This proves that Job did not, as many maintain, regard the grave as a mere sleep. 3.-- Months of comfortless misfortune. I am made to possess-- literally, "to be heir to." Irony. "To be heir to," is usually a matter of joy; but here it is the entail of an involuntary and dismal inheritance. Months-- for days, to express its long duration. Appointed-- literally, "they have numbered to me"; marking well the unavoidable doom assigned to him.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4595"/><div sID="gen6663" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4595"/><hi type="bold">15. Umbreit translates, "So that I could wish to strangle myself--</hi>dead by my own hands." He softens this idea of Job's harboring the thought of suicide, by representing it as entertained only in agonizing dreams, and immediately repudiated with horror in <reference osisRef="Job.7.16">Job 7:16</reference>, "Yet that (self-strangling) I loathe." This is forcible and graphic. Perhaps the meaning is simply, "My soul chooses (even) strangling (or any violent death) rather than my life," literally, "my bones" (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.10">Psa 35:10</reference>); that is, rather than the wasted and diseased skeleton, left to him. In this view, "I loathe it" (<reference osisRef="Job.7.16">Job 7:16</reference>) refers to his life. <div eID="gen6663" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4597"/><div sID="gen6665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4597"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Ps.8.4">Psa 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.3">144:3</reference>). Job means, "What is man that thou shouldst make him [of so much importance], and that thou shouldst expend such attention [or, heart-thought] upon him" as to make him the subject of so severe trials? Job ought rather to have reasoned from God's condescending so far to notice man as to try him, that there must be a wise and loving purpose in trial. David uses the same words, in their right application, to express wonder that God should do so much as He does for insignificant man. Christians who know God manifest in the man Christ Jesus may use them still more. <div eID="gen6665" type="x-p"/>

I have sinned--</hi>Yet what sin can I do against ("to," <reference osisRef="Job.35.6">Job 35:6</reference>) thee (of such a nature that thou shouldst jealously watch and deprive me of all strength, as if thou didst fear me)? Yet thou art one who hast men ever in view, ever watchest them--O thou Watcher (<reference osisRef="Job.7.12">Job 7:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.14">Da 9:14</reference>) of men. Job had borne with patience his trials, as sent by God (<reference osisRef="Job.1.21">Job 1:21</reference>; 2:10); only his reason cannot reconcile the ceaseless continuance of his mental and bodily pains with his ideas of the divine nature.<div eID="gen6668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">set me as a mark--</hi>Wherefore dost thou make me thy point of attack? that is, ever assail me with new pains? [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.12">La 3:12</reference>). <div eID="gen6669" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4601"/><div sID="gen6670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4601"/><hi type="bold">21. for now--</hi>very soon.<div eID="gen6670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the morning--</hi>not the resurrection; for then Job will be found. It is a figure, from one seeking a sick man in the morning, and finding he has died in the night. So Job implies that, if God does not help him at once, it will be too late, for he will be gone. The reason why God does not give an immediate sense of pardon to awakened sinners is that they think they have a claim on God for it. <chapter eID="Job.7"/>
